objective.statement: Understand double sharps and double flats, how long they last and how a natural sign cancels them.
successCriteria: I know the double sharp raises a note by two semitones and the double flat lowers it by two.
I can name and write notes with double signs.
I know a double sign lasts to the end of the bar and a natural sign cancels it.

explanation.text: A sharp raises a note by one semitone and a flat lowers it by one. Sometimes a note that is already sharp must go higher still. The double sharp (𝄪) raises a note by two semitones, a whole tone, and the double flat (𝄫) lowers it by two. Each is simply two single signs together.

music.textAlternative: A treble stave with three semibreves on the same line: F, F sharp and F double sharp.

explanation.caption: F, F♯ and F𝄪 climb by a semitone each. F𝄪 sounds the same as G.

explanation.text: A double sign is part of the note's name, so spelling matters. F𝄪 sounds like G, but it is called F because of the letter on the stave. Likewise B𝄫 sounds like A, and E𝄫 like D. Later you will see why a composer chooses the double sign: the letter names have to stay in order.

Like any accidental, a double sign lasts until the end of the bar, on the same line or space. A natural sign (♮) cancels it, and the note is plain again. At the barline an accidental ends and the key signature takes over again.

music.textAlternative: One bar of 4/4: F double sharp, A, C, then F natural.

explanation.caption: The natural sign before the last F cancels the double sharp.

explanation.text: 𝄪 = up two semitones, 𝄫 = down two. A double sign lasts to the barline. A natural sign cancels it. Older music sometimes uses ♮♯ to go from 𝄪 to a single sharp; this course only asks about the natural sign.

music.textAlternative: A treble stave with F and then F double sharp.

steps: Play F. Play F sharp: one key higher.
F double sharp is one more key higher: the key you call G.
Same sound as G, but written as F with two sharps.
demonstration.textAlternative: F then F double sharp, which sounds the same as G.

guided.prompt: A double flat lowers a note by how many semitones?

1.reason: That is what a single flat does. A double sign is two single signs together.

3.reason: A double sign is worth exactly two semitones: two single signs, one semitone each.

4.reason: Four semitones is a whole major third. A double sign is worth just two semitones.

hints: A double sign moves a note two semitones.
A double flat is two flats together.

mistakes.accidental-forgotten: An accidental keeps working for the rest of the bar on that line or space.
mistakes.accidental-carried-over-barline: A bar-line cancels accidentals — unless the note is tied across it.
mistakes.key-signature-ignored: Don't forget the key signature: it affects every note with that letter name.
mistakes.different-octave-assumed: An accidental only affects notes on the same line or space — not the same letter in another octave.
mistakes.tie-over-barline: A tie carries the accidental into the next bar, but only for the tied note.
mistakes.double-as-single: A double sharp or double flat moves a note by two semitones, twice as far as a single sign.
mistakes.sign-direction: Sharps raise a note and flats lower it; the double signs do the same twice over.
mistakes.double-ignored: The double sign changes the sound by two semitones: it cannot be ignored.
mistakes.not-two-semitones: Count exactly two semitones from the plain note.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Go through the bar from the start, tracking each accidental.

mistakes.counted-from-top: Lines and spaces are counted from the bottom of the stave upwards.
mistakes.off-by-step: You're one step away. Find a note you know for certain and count up or down from it.
mistakes.ledger-miscount: Count the ledger lines one at a time, from the stave outwards.
mistakes.accidental-ignored: The letter is right, but check for a sharp, flat or natural — in the key signature or in front of the note.

guided.prompt: A note has been written with a double flat. Later in the same bar the same note must be plain again, with no sharp or flat at all. Which sign is written before it?

sharp.reason: A flat would leave the note altered. To make it plain, cancel the alteration with a natural sign.

flat.reason: A flat would lower the note. To make it plain, cancel the alteration with a natural sign.

double-sharp.reason: That is another double sign, which alters the note again. A natural sign cancels the alteration.

hints: An accidental lasts to the barline; a natural sign cancels it.
A natural sign cancels any earlier sharp, flat, double sharp or double flat on that note.

feedback.correct: Yes: a natural sign cancels the double sign.

provenance.notes: Original wording. Follows Grade 4 outcome 8 and First Steps Grade 4 section 5 (p. 83, read in the PDF) for the signs and what they do. The book does not cover cancelling; the cancellation material here is original. OPEN_QUESTIONS Q9: only the unambiguous convention is asked (a natural sign gives a natural note). The older natural-plus-sharp way of reducing a double sharp to a single one is mentioned once in the tip and never asked; a teacher must confirm which convention to teach.
